strengths: The motivation to leverage intrinsic multi-head self-attention for coordinate-free GUI grounding is sound and avoids the overhead of introducing separate grounding heads or complex multi-stage warm-up training required by prior work like GUI-Actor.
The use of an <ANCHOR> token neatly simplifies the query-to-visual aggregation problem, providing a single surrogate token whose attention map over visual patches can be directly supervised.

The empirical results are solid across multiple GUI benchmarks (ScreenSpot-v2, ScreenSpot-Pro, OSWorld-G), demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to peer 3B models and even some larger 7B models with modest training data scale (85k screenshots / 259k instructions).

Thorough ablation studies validate each component of the proposed framework, including the anchored token, visual-sink query token selection strategies, head weighting schemes, and the zoom-in inference parameters.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is relatively incremental: using attention maps for GUI grounding was pioneered by TAG, supervising special tokens for localization is common (e.g., GUI-Actor), and the Gaussian/IoU patch labeling is adopted directly from GUI-G2.

The visual-sink query token selection and head weighting mechanisms are somewhat heuristic, relying on multiple layers of ad-hoc similarity and cumulative attention metrics. Moreover, the performance delta between uniform head weighting and visual-sink weighting in Table 4 is modest on ScreenSpot-v2 (88.92% vs. 89.39%).

A substantial portion of the headline performance leap on ScreenSpot-Pro (from 45.2% to 58.6%) stems from the test-time two-step zoom-in crop heuristic, which is an inference engineering trick rather than an intrinsic contribution of the attention-alignment training framework.

The manuscript claims that supervising the <ANCHOR> token avoids degrading the MLLM's general multimodal capabilities (e.g., image captioning, general VQA), but does not provide any empirical evaluation on standard general vision-language benchmarks before and after fine-tuning to substantiate this claim.

strengths: The proposed method formulates coordinate-free GUI visual grounding by directly supervising intrinsic multi-head self-attention matrices via an <ANCHOR> token, avoiding the need for auxiliary modules or multi-stage warm-up training required by prior embedding-based approaches like GUI-Actor.
The head-weighting scheme based on visual-sink query tokens provides an effective and intuitive way to prioritize functionally relevant attention heads using hidden-state query-visual similarities.

The framework exhibits strong data efficiency and empirical performance: trained on only ~85k screenshots (259k instruction pairs), GUI-AIMA-3B achieves competitive or superior performance compared to 7B and 72B models on ScreenSpot-v2, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G.

The ablation study is thorough, dissecting the benefits of the <ANCHOR> token, the visual-sink query token selection criteria (layer-wise vs. global uniform, top-K), the head weighting formulations, and the center/overlap-aware patch labeling.
The coordinate-free patch prediction lends itself naturally to a two-step zoom-in inference pipeline without additional fine-tuning, yielding significant accuracy gains on high-resolution displays.
weaknesses: The two-step zoom-in inference requires an additional forward pass over the cropped region. The paper does not provide runtime latency or computational overhead (FLOPs/FPS) comparisons against standard autoregressive coordinate generation.

The terminology 'visual-sink query token' could lead to slight confusion with the standard LLM literature on 'attention sinks' (which typically denotes initial tokens absorbing residual softmax probability mass). Clarifying this distinction earlier in Section 3.4 would improve readability.

Supervising and backpropagating through attention matrices across all layers and heads can introduce non-trivial GPU memory overhead during training compared to standard language modeling cross-entropy loss; quantitative discussion or benchmarking of training memory/speed tradeoffs is missing.
The evaluation is restricted to single-element grounding; its applicability to full-trajectory GUI agents involving multi-step planning and tool usage is not demonstrated.

strengths: Sound and elegant formulation: Supervising the intrinsic multi-head self-attention of MLLMs directly via a dedicated <ANCHOR> token avoids the need for auxiliary projection modules or multi-stage alignment heads (as in GUI-Actor) while circumventing noisy per-query-token attention aggregation.

Well-motivated head weighting: The proposed visual-sink query token selection dynamically identifies heads carrying strong semantic query-visual interactions from hidden states, providing an effective and principled way to aggregate multi-head attention maps.

Strong performance and data efficiency: With only ~85k training screenshots (259k instructions), GUI-AIMA-3B achieves SOTA performance among 3B-scale models and rivals 7B+ models on ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, and OSWorld-G.

Comprehensive ablation study: The ablation experiments cleanly isolate and validate the benefits of the <ANCHOR> token, head-weighting strategies, soft Gaussian patch-wise labels, and the zoom-in inference step.
weaknesses: Lack of inference latency analysis: The optional two-step zoom-in strategy provides a substantial performance boost (+11.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro), but requires a secondary forward pass on a cropped patch. The paper does not provide runtime, latency, or throughput metrics comparing 1-step vs. 2-step inference against coordinate-generating baselines.

Evaluation limited to a single MLLM architecture: All main experiments and ablations are conducted solely on Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct. Demonstrating applicability to other backbones (e.g., Llama-based or InternVL-based architectures) would better confirm the generalizability of intrinsic attention supervision across model families.

Limitation to point-based click grounding: The current framework focuses primarily on single click-point localization (patch heatmap center). Extending or evaluating the method for multi-point grounding or precise bounding box regression is left as future work, which slightly restricts its scope in broader visual grounding settings.

strengths: Clean and well-motivated formulation: By placing a learnable <ANCHOR> token at the end of the input sequence under causal self-attention, the method elegantly circumvents impractical query token-wise attention aggregation and eliminates the need for auxiliary grounding heads or separate warm-up stages (e.g., compared to GUI-Actor).

Principled head-weighting mechanism: The use of representation-space hidden-state similarity to identify visual-sink query tokens provides an effective, head-agnostic proxy to dynamically weight grounding-relevant attention heads while avoiding disturbance to general pretrained heads.

Strong empirical performance and data efficiency: GUI-AIMA-3B achieves state-of-the-art results among 3B-scale models across multiple challenging GUI grounding benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, MMBench-GUI-L2, UI-Vision) using only ~509k training samples, remaining competitive with much larger 7B/72B baselines.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: The paper provides insightful analyses, including detailed ablations of query aggregation, head weighting variants, convergence curves (Fig. 5), attention head pruning (Fig. 6), and error recovery breakdown across offset distances in the zoom-in stage (Table 6).
weaknesses: Gradient flow and optimization clarity regarding head weights: In Eq. (2) and Eq. (3), the head weights $w_{l,h}$ are computed dynamically from attention maps. While Appendix Table 10 evaluates a 'stop-grad on w' ablation, the main text does not clarify whether $w_{l,h}$ is treated as detached or differentiated through during end-to-end training, nor does it discuss potential training stability implications.

Semantic role of visual-sink tokens: Fig. 4 indicates that the selected visual-sink tokens are predominantly punctuation and stopwords (e.g., 'the', '\n', '.', 'a'). While the authors conceptualize them as functional attention sinks that aggregate global context, the paper lacks a deeper mechanistic explanation for why stopword-to-image similarity reliably captures task-specific grounding relevance over semantically rich entity tokens.

Inference latency trade-off: The two-step zoom-in procedure provides substantial accuracy gains on high-resolution screens, but effectively requires two forward passes. In real-time computer-use agent scenarios where inference speed is critical, the operational cost of this second pass should be more thoroughly discussed alongside wall-clock latency.

Presentation and minor omissions: There are minor presentation oversights, such as an incomplete project page link in the Abstract ('Project page: .') and limited discussion on handling fine-grained multiple UI elements co-located within a single visual patch prior to zoom-in.

strengths: Well-motivated approach: Direct supervision on the intrinsic multi-head self-attention of MLLMs for GUI grounding provides a clean, coordinate-free formulation that avoids textual coordinate formatting issues and eliminates the need for separate grounding heads or complex multi-stage warm-up training.

Clever and lightweight architectural design: Using an appended <ANCHOR> token as a context summarizer neatly bypasses explicit token-wise aggregation under causal attention, and extracting attention only for the query/anchor rows preserves the efficiency of FlashAttention with minimal computational overhead (~4.2%).

Principled head weighting: Grounding-relevant attention head reweighting using 'visual-sink' query tokens based on representation-space similarity is intuitive and empirically proven to reduce noise from irrelevant heads and stabilize early training.

Strong performance and data efficiency: GUI-AIMA-3B achieves impressive accuracy across multiple challenging desktop, mobile, and web benchmarks (e.g., 61.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 92.1% on ScreenSpot-v2, 68.1% on OSWorld-G) while being trained on only ~509k samples, outperforming or matching much larger or more heavily trained SFT/RL models.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: The paper includes extensive ablations dissecting the coordinate-free design, head-weighting strategies, patch labeling, and the mechanics of the plug-and-play two-step zoom-in refinement.
weaknesses: Mechanistic clarity on visual sinks: Figure 4 shows that the top selected 'visual-sink' tokens are predominantly stopwords and punctuation (e.g., 'the', '\n', '.'). While the authors hypothesize that these tokens act as functional proxies for cross-modal interaction, it is well documented that LLMs exhibit generic 'attention sink' or representation collapse behaviors on punctuation. A deeper explanation or analysis of whether this represents semantic cross-modal alignment versus an artifact of transformer hidden-state geometry would strengthen the paper.

Inference latency trade-off of two-step zoom-in: The zoom-in stage brings large gains (e.g., +7.7% on ScreenSpot-Pro), but requires a second crop-and-forward pass. Although standard in high-resolution GUI grounding, the paper would benefit from explicitly reporting the end-to-end latency and compute trade-off compared to single-pass coordinate-predicting baselines.

Limitation to single-target grounding: The current <ANCHOR> formulation is inherently designed for single-element grounding per forward pass. While discussed briefly in Appendix D, handling multi-element detection or multi-target instructions in a single pass remains an unaddressed limitation of the current architecture.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear limitation of existing MLLM-based GUI grounding approaches (which typically rely on clumsy textual coordinate generation or auxiliary grounding heads) by directly supervising the intrinsic multi-head self-attention (MHSA) of the base MLLM in a coordinate-free manner.

The technical design is elegant and lightweight: appending a learnable <ANCHOR> token neatly sidesteps manual query token aggregation under causal masking, while the visual-sink query token selection mechanism offers an effective, head-agnostic proxy to reweight grounding-relevant attention heads without introducing heavy extra modules.

The method demonstrates remarkable data efficiency and strong empirical results, achieving state-of-the-art performance among 3B models across five benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, and MMBench-GUI-L2) with only ~509k fine-tuning samples.

The patch-level attention formulation naturally facilitates a simple, training-free two-step zoom-in inference scheme that effectively mitigates offset errors on dense, high-resolution desktop screens.
Comprehensive experimental analysis and ablations convincingly substantiate the contributions of the anchor token, visual-sink selection, head reweighting, and distance-aware patch labeling.
weaknesses: The current formulation is tailored primarily to single-target point grounding; as noted in the appendix, extending the single <ANCHOR> token to multi-element grounding or dense element detection remains unexplored and non-trivial.

The reliance on 'visual-sink' query tokens (frequently stopwords or punctuation like 'the', '\n', and '.' as shown in Fig. 4) lacks deeper theoretical grounding; while empirical performance is good, a more rigorous justification for why non-semantic syntactic sink tokens best identify grounding-specialized attention heads would strengthen the work.

The two-step zoom-in inference inherently incurs additional computational and latency costs from the secondary forward pass, but the trade-offs regarding real-time agent execution speed are only briefly analyzed.
